body.heading: Small and often beats big and rare
paragraphs: A two-minute check-in is exactly what it sounds like: a short message or moment that asks, properly, how someone is. “How did the interview go?” on the day of the interview is worth more than a long catch-up three months later.
The secret ingredient is remembering. You are not really sending a message; you are sending proof that their life stayed in your mind after they left the room.

body.heading: Make it easy to answer
paragraphs: A check-in should never feel like homework. One question, answerable in a sentence, is plenty. “Thinking of you — dentist done?” invites a reply; a twelve-part questionnaire invites a delay.
And accept the short answer warmly. “Fine, thanks” with a wave is still a completed check-in. The channel stays open for the day it is really needed.

body.heading: Rhythm over inspiration
paragraphs: Pick a rhythm you can keep: Monday mornings, the first of the month, the anniversary of something only you two remember. Regularity turns a nice thought into a structure people can rely on.
It does not need to be equal. Some seasons you will carry the rhythm; some seasons they will. That is how long friendships actually work.

takeaway: Check in small, check in often, and let remembering be the message.
